love-maps.summary: Happy couples keep a detailed, up-to-date picture of each other's world: worries, hopes, friends and history. Knowing each other this well seems to help couples weather big changes like a new baby, and because people keep changing, it's worth asking again.
sources: Gottman, J. M., & Silver, N. (1999). The seven principles for making marriage work. Crown.

Shapiro, A. F., Gottman, J. M., & Carrère, S. (2000). The baby and the marriage: Identifying factors that buffer against decline in marital satisfaction after the first baby arrives. Journal of Family Psychology, 14(1), 59–70.

appreciation.summary: Noticing and saying what you value in each other matters. People who feel appreciated tend to appreciate their partner back, respond more kindly and stay more committed, and couples who tell their story with fondness are more likely to stay together.
sources: Algoe, S. B. (2012). Find, remind, and bind: The functions of gratitude in everyday relationships. Social and Personality Psychology Compass, 6(6), 455–469.

Gordon, A. M., Impett, E. A., Kogan, A., Oveis, C., & Keltner, D. (2012). To have and to hold: Gratitude promotes relationship maintenance in intimate bonds. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 103(2), 257–274.

Buehlman, K. T., Gottman, J. M., & Katz, L. F. (1992). How a couple views their past predicts their future: Predicting divorce from an oral history interview. Journal of Family Psychology, 5(3–4), 295–318.

connection.summary: Love is built in small moments: a shared joke, a question about someone's day, real excitement about good news. Turning toward these everyday bids, especially with enthusiasm, goes with warmer, more affectionate relationships, even during disagreements.
sources: Driver, J. L., & Gottman, J. M. (2004). Daily marital interactions and positive affect during marital conflict among newlywed couples. Family Process, 43(3), 301–314.

Reis, H. T., Clark, M. S., & Holmes, J. G. (2004). Perceived partner responsiveness as an organizing construct in the study of intimacy and closeness. In D. J. Mashek & A. P. Aron (Eds.), Handbook of closeness and intimacy (pp. 201–225). Lawrence Erlbaum Associates.

Gable, S. L., Reis, H. T., Impett, E. A., & Asher, E. R. (2004). What do you do when things go right? The intrapersonal and interpersonal benefits of sharing positive events. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 87(2), 228–245.

growth.summary: Couples feel closer when they help each other learn, try new things and become who they want to be. Doing something new and a little challenging together gave couples a short-term lift, and being seen as your best self helps you grow toward it.
sources: Aron, A., & Aron, E. N. (1986). Love and the expansion of self: Understanding attraction and satisfaction. Hemisphere.

Aron, A., Norman, C. C., Aron, E. N., McKenna, C., & Heyman, R. E. (2000). Couples' shared participation in novel and arousing activities and experienced relationship quality. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 78(2), 273–284.

Drigotas, S. M., Rusbult, C. E., Wieselquist, J., & Whitton, S. W. (1999). Close partner as sculptor of the ideal self: Behavioral affirmation and the Michelangelo phenomenon. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 77(2), 293–323.

conflict.summary: Every couple disagrees, and some disagreements never fully go away. How you talk matters most: criticism, contempt, defensiveness and shutting down are warning signs, while looking at a fight the way a kind, neutral observer would helped keep marriages from sliding.
sources: Gottman, J. M., & Levenson, R. W. (1992). Marital processes predictive of later dissolution: Behavior, physiology, and health. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 63(2), 221–233.
Gottman, J. M., & Silver, N. (1999). The seven principles for making marriage work. Crown.

Finkel, E. J., Slotter, E. B., Luchies, L. B., Walton, G. M., & Gross, J. J. (2013). A brief intervention to promote conflict reappraisal preserves marital quality over time. Psychological Science, 24(8), 1595–1601.

security.summary: Feeling confident that your partner will be there for you is at the heart of adult love. A well-tested couples therapy built on this idea helps partners say what they need to feel safe and close. These prompts borrow that spirit, but they aren't therapy.
sources: Hazan, C., & Shaver, P. (1987). Romantic love conceptualized as an attachment process. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 52(3), 511–524.
Wiebe, S. A., & Johnson, S. M. (2016). A review of the research in emotionally focused therapy for couples. Family Process, 55(3), 390–407.

Rathgeber, M., Bürkner, P.-C., Schiller, E.-M., & Holling, H. (2019). The efficacy of emotionally focused couples therapy and behavioral couples therapy: A meta-analysis. Journal of Marital and Family Therapy, 45(3), 447–463.

trust.summary: Trust grows when you see your partner choose “us” over “me”: small sacrifices, compromises, showing up. Commitment is stronger when you're satisfied, have built a life together and aren't looking elsewhere, and committed couples are more likely to last.
sources: Rusbult, C. E. (1980). Commitment and satisfaction in romantic associations: A test of the investment model. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 16(2), 172–186.
Le, B., & Agnew, C. R. (2003). Commitment and its theorized determinants: A meta-analysis of the Investment Model. Personal Relationships, 10(1), 37–57.

Wieselquist, J., Rusbult, C. E., Foster, C. A., & Agnew, C. R. (1999). Commitment, pro-relationship behavior, and trust in close relationships. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 77(5), 942–966.

checkin.summary: A regular relationship check-up, noticing what's going well and what needs care, helped married couples feel closer, more accepted and less distressed in a rigorous two-year study. Structured online programs can also help couples who are struggling.
sources: Cordova, J. V., Fleming, C. J. E., Morrill, M. I., Hawrilenko, M., Sollenberger, J. W., Harp, A. G., Gray, T. D., Darling, E. V., Blair, J. M., Meade, A. E., & Wachs, K. (2014). The Marriage Checkup: A randomized controlled trial of annual relationship health checkups. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 82(4), 592–604.

Doss, B. D., Cicila, L. N., Georgia, E. J., Roddy, M. K., Nowlan, K. M., Benson, L. A., & Christensen, A. (2016). A randomized controlled trial of the web-based OurRelationship program: Effects on relationship and individual functioning. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 84(4), 285–296.

marriage.summary: Commitment has two sides: wanting a future together, and finding it hard to leave. Deciding on big steps together, rather than sliding into them, is thought to build the first kind. Talking through what marriage means to you is the heart of programs that modestly help couples.
sources: Stanley, S. M., & Markman, H. J. (1992). Assessing commitment in personal relationships. Journal of Marriage and the Family, 54(3), 595–608.
Stanley, S. M., Rhoades, G. K., & Markman, H. J. (2006). Sliding versus deciding: Inertia and the premarital cohabitation effect. Family Relations, 55(4), 499–509.

Hawkins, A. J., Blanchard, V. L., Baldwin, S. A., & Fawcett, E. B. (2008). Does marriage and relationship education work? A meta-analytic study. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 76(5), 723–734.

kids.summary: On average, relationship satisfaction dips a little after a baby arrives, most of all for new mothers. Couples who stay fond of each other and keep up with each other's inner lives tend to weather it best, so it helps to talk about hopes and worries early.
sources: Twenge, J. M., Campbell, W. K., & Foster, C. A. (2003). Parenthood and marital satisfaction: A meta-analytic review. Journal of Marriage and Family, 65(3), 574–583.

Doss, B. D., Rhoades, G. K., Stanley, S. M., & Markman, H. J. (2009). The effect of the transition to parenthood on relationship quality: An 8-year prospective study. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 96(3), 601–619.

Shapiro, A. F., Gottman, J. M., & Carrère, S. (2000). The baby and the marriage: Identifying factors that buffer against decline in marital satisfaction after the first baby arrives. Journal of Family Psychology, 14(1), 59–70.

home.summary: Who does what at home is shaped by time, money and expectations, and feeling that it's fair matters more and more, even for couples' sex lives. Living together before marriage is linked to fewer divorces early in marriage but more later, so moving in deserves a real talk.
sources: Lachance-Grzela, M., & Bouchard, G. (2010). Why do women do the lion's share of housework? A decade of research. Sex Roles, 63(11–12), 767–780.
Carlson, D. L., Miller, A. J., Sassler, S., & Hanson, S. (2016). The gendered division of housework and couples' sexual relationships: A reexamination. Journal of Marriage and Family, 78(4), 975–995.
Rosenfeld, M. J., & Roesler, K. (2019). Cohabitation experience and cohabitation's association with marital dissolution. Journal of Marriage and Family, 81(1), 42–58.

money.summary: Money arguments aren't always the most common, but they tend to be the stickiest: harder to handle, more repetitive and less often resolved. They also predict divorce more than other disagreements. Sharing what money means to you, calmly and early, can help.
sources: Dew, J., Britt, S., & Huston, S. (2012). Examining the relationship between financial issues and divorce. Family Relations, 61(4), 615–628.
Papp, L. M., Cummings, E. M., & Goeke-Morey, M. C. (2009). For richer, for poorer: Money as a topic of marital conflict in the home. Family Relations, 58(1), 91–103.

origins.summary: The families we grew up in shape how we love, argue and commit, but they don't decide our fate. Parents' conflict and divorce can echo in their children's relationships, and in-law ties matter too. Sharing family stories helps you understand each other's defaults.
sources: Amato, P. R., & Booth, A. (2001). The legacy of parents' marital discord: Consequences for children's marital quality. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 81(4), 627–638.
Amato, P. R., & DeBoer, D. D. (2001). The transmission of marital instability across generations: Relationship skills or commitment to marriage? Journal of Marriage and Family, 63(4), 1038–1051.
Orbuch, T. L., Bauermeister, J. A., Brown, E., & McKinley, B.-D. (2013). Early family ties and marital stability over 16 years: The context of race and gender. Family Relations, 62(2), 255–268.

dreams.summary: Partners who encourage each other's goals, cheering on without taking over, help each other feel happier, more confident and more likely to succeed. Supporting each other's dreams also goes with a happier relationship. Knowing those dreams is the first step.
sources: Feeney, B. C. (2004). A secure base: Responsive support of goal strivings and exploration in adult intimate relationships. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 87(5), 631–648.

Brunstein, J. C., Dangelmayer, G., & Schultheiss, O. C. (1996). Personal goals and social support in close relationships: Effects on relationship mood and marital satisfaction. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 71(5), 1006–1019.

meaning.summary: Shared rituals and traditions, like a weekly dinner, a holiday custom or the way you say goodnight, are linked with happier marriages. Couples who see their bond as sacred report stronger marriages too. Your own sense of meaning can be religious or not.
sources: Fiese, B. H., Tomcho, T. J., Douglas, M., Josephs, K., Poltrock, S., & Baker, T. (2002). A review of 50 years of research on naturally occurring family routines and rituals: Cause for celebration? Journal of Family Psychology, 16(4), 381–390.

Mahoney, A., Pargament, K. I., Jewell, T., Swank, A. B., Scott, E., Emery, E., & Rye, M. (1999). Marriage and the spiritual realm: The role of proximal and distal religious constructs in marital functioning. Journal of Family Psychology, 13(3), 321–338.

stress.summary: Stress from work, money or health easily spills into a relationship and makes small things feel bigger. Couples who share their stress and tackle it as a team tend to be more satisfied, so saying “I'm stressed, here's what would help” is worth practicing.
sources: Bodenmann, G. (2005). Dyadic coping and its significance for marital functioning. In T. A. Revenson, K. Kayser, & G. Bodenmann (Eds.), Couples coping with stress: Emerging perspectives on dyadic coping (pp. 33–49). American Psychological Association.
Falconier, M. K., Jackson, J. B., Hilpert, P., & Bodenmann, G. (2015). Dyadic coping and relationship satisfaction: A meta-analysis. Clinical Psychology Review, 42, 28–46.

Neff, L. A., & Karney, B. R. (2009). Stress and reactivity to daily relationship experiences: How stress hinders adaptive processes in marriage. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 97(3), 435–450.

intimacy.summary: Talking openly about sex, including what you enjoy and what you'd like more of, goes with a better sex life and a happier relationship, and how well you talk matters more than how often. Caring about meeting your partner's needs also helps keep desire alive.
sources: Mallory, A. B., Stanton, A. M., & Handy, A. B. (2019). Couples' sexual communication and dimensions of sexual function: A meta-analysis. The Journal of Sex Research, 56(7), 882–898.
Mallory, A. B. (2022). Dimensions of couples' sexual communication, relationship satisfaction, and sexual satisfaction: A meta-analysis. Journal of Family Psychology, 36(3), 358–371.

Muise, A., Impett, E. A., Kogan, A., & Desmarais, S. (2013). Keeping the spark alive: Being motivated to meet a partner's sexual needs sustains sexual desire in long-term romantic relationships. Social Psychological and Personality Science, 4(3), 267–273.
